If the special vertex is decorated by
\delta_{0,A}
or
\psi_{i}
, then
\delta_{res}
vanishes.
Note that
\delta_{res}
is homogeneous of degree 1.

The part
\delta_{split}
splits undecorated vertices as usual.
When the special vertex is split this is done as follows:

•

If decorated by
\psi_{i}
the special vertex is again split as in (
13
) on p.
13
.

•

If decorated by
\delta_{0,S}
the special vertex is split as in (
14
) on p.
14
.

•

If decorated by
E_{ij}
some subset
S
of half-edges is split off that does not contain both
i
and
j
(but might contain neither of them), as shown:

(26)

Proposition 5.2
.

The differential on
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
is well-defined and squares to zero.

24
).

27
) agrees with that in (
28
), with the sign due to interchanging the two edges. The second term agrees with the second term in (
28
) due to the relations. Each summand in the third term appears twice, with opposite sign, by applying
\delta_{split}
to two different terms in the sum appearing in (
24
).
The verification that the differential respects the fourth loop relation is similar.

Now we must check that the differential squares to zero. Suppose
\Gamma
is a generator for
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{2}_{g,n}
. We must show:

(\delta_{split}+\delta_{res})^{2}\Gamma=\delta_{split}^{2}\Gamma+(\delta_{split}\delta_{res}+\delta_{res}\delta_{split})\Gamma=0.

The argument for cancellation of terms that arise from splitting non-special vertices is identical to the proof that differential squares to zero on the ordinary commutative graph complex. The same argument adapts easily to cases where the special vertex is decorated with
\psi_{i}
or
\delta_{0,A}
, because in these cases
\delta_{res}=0
.

Suppose the special vertex is decorated by
E_{ij}
.
The standard argument shows that
\delta_{split}^{2}\Gamma=0
. It remains to show
(\delta_{split}\delta_{res}+\delta_{res}\delta_{split})\Gamma=0
.
Applying
\delta_{res}
to the right-hand side of (
26
) gives
(-1)^{e+1}
times

(29)

We need to compare this to
\delta_{split}
applied to the right-hand side of (
25
). The fourth and seventh terms together match
\delta_{split}
applied to the second term of (
25
), with opposite sign. Likewise, the second and the eighth term of (
29
) match
\delta_{split}
applied to the first term of (
25
). The cancellation of the remaining terms is similar.
∎

Proposition 5.3
.

There is a quasi-isomorphism

\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}

that sets
E_{ij}
to zero and imposes the relation
\psi_{i}+\psi_{j}-\displaystyle\sum_{i\in S,j\in S^{c}}\delta_{0,S}
.

Proof.

We first verify that this projection is a well-defined map of complexes. It clearly respects the differential on all generators where the special vertex is decorated by
\psi
or
\delta_{0,A}
. Consider a generator
\Gamma\in\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
whose special vertex is decorated by
E_{ij}
. Then
\delta_{split}\Gamma
also has an
E_{ij}
-decorated special vertex and is hence sent to zero.
Furthermore
\delta_{res}\Gamma
is sent to zero since its special vertex is just decorated by the relation between
\psi
- and
\delta
-classes.

To see that this projection is a quasi-isomorphism, we filter both sides by the number of vertices and consider the associated spectral sequences.
We claim that the map
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{2}_{g,n}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
induces a quasi-isomorphism already on the associated graded complex.
Proceeding as in Section
4.3
one can see it therefore suffices to consider the complex associated to the special vertex.
The differential on the associated graded of
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{2}_{g,n}
is zero, and the differential on the associated graded of
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{2}_{g,n}
does not add any edges. We can therefore consider separate cases according to whether or not there is a loop at the special vertex.

If there is no loop, then the loop relations listed above do not come into play, and the statement boils down to Proposition
3.5
, which says that

\bigoplus_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\mathbb{Q}E_{ij}\to\Big(\bigoplus_{1\leq i\leq k}\mathbb{Q}\psi_{i}\Big)\oplus\bigoplus\mathbb{Q}\delta_{0,S}

is a resolution of
H^{2}(\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{0,k})
.

It remains to consider the case where there is a loop at the special vertex. Let
t,t^{\prime}
denote the last two marked points on
\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{0,k+2}
. We must show that the complex

(30)

\bigoplus_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\mathbb{Q}E_{ij}\to\bigoplus_{A\subset\{1,\ldots,k\}}\mathbb{Q}\delta_{0,A\cup\{t\}},\to H^{2}(\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{0,k+2})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}/\sim

is exact, where
\sim
is the quotient by the loop relations
\delta_{0,A}=0
for
A\subset\{1,\ldots,k\}
. To see this, we begin by taking the
\mathbb{S}_{2}
-coinvariants of the resolution of
H^{2}(\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{0,k+2})
from Proposition
3.5
. Then the
\mathbb{S}_{2}
-coinvariant space of the first term
\bigoplus\mathbb{Q}E_{ij}
has a basis consisting of

E_{ij},\ 1\leq i<j\leq k;\quad\quad\quad E_{it},\ 1\leq i\leq k;\quad\quad\quad E_{tt^{\prime}}.

Similarly, the
\mathbb{S}_{2}
-coinvariant space of the second term
(\bigoplus\mathbb{Q}\psi_{i})\oplus(\bigoplus\mathbb{Q}\delta_{0,A})
has a basis consisting of

\psi_{i},\ 1\leq i\leq k;\quad\quad\psi_{t};\quad\quad\delta_{0,A},\ A\subset\{1,\ldots,k\},\ |S|\geq 2;\quad\quad\delta_{0,A\cup\{t\}},\ A\subset\{1,\ldots,k\},\ |A|\geq 1,\ |A^{c}|\geq 1.

By Lemma
4.4
, the subspace spanned by the basis elements
\delta_{0,A}
, for
\ A\subset\{1,\ldots,k\}
,
|A|\geq 2
maps isomorphically onto its image in
H^{2}(\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{0,k+2})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}
, which is precisely the span of the loop relations. We can then use
E_{it}
to eliminate
\psi_{i}
and
E_{tt^{\prime}}
to eliminate
\psi_{t}
and see that (
30
) is exact, as required.
∎

5.3.
Completing the zig-zag

We now complete the zig-zag from
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
to
X_{g,n}
by producing a quasi-isomorphism

\Phi:\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}\xrightarrow{\sim}X_{g,n}.

Let
\Gamma
be a graph in
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}
with
e
structural edges. Say that the half-edges incident to external vertices are
legs
.

•

If the special vertex of
\Gamma
is decorated by
\delta_{0,A}
we define
\Phi(\Gamma)=0
.

•

If the special vertex of
\Gamma
is decorated by
E_{ij}
, then we let
\Phi(\Gamma)
be the marked graph obtained by deleting the special vertex, making the half-edges incident to the special vertex into legs, and decorating the external vertices on
i,j
by
\omega
and the other newly created external vertices by
\epsilon
.

(31)

\omega

(-1)^{e}
.

In both cases (
32
) and (

),
\Phi(\Gamma)
has one more edge than
\Gamma
. We may assume, without loss of generality, that the decorated edge (of which
i
is one half-edge) is the first in the ordering of edges. Then we order the structural edges in
\Phi(\Gamma)
such that the edge containing
i
is first, the edge containing the opposite half-edge of
i
is second, and the relative order of the remaining edges is unchanged.

Lemma 5.4
.

The map
\Phi
is a map of complexes.

Proof.

It is clear that the map
\Phi
respects the degrees and genera and is hence a well-defined map of graded vector spaces. We need to verify that it commutes with the differentials,

\delta\Phi(\Gamma)=\Phi(\delta\Gamma).

Recall that the differential on
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}
is
\delta=\delta_{split}+\delta_{res}
, while the differential on
X_{g,n}
is
\delta=\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}
.
We furthermore decompose the operation
\delta_{split}
on
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}
into two terms,

\delta_{split}=\delta_{split}^{s}+\delta_{split}^{o},

with
\delta_{split}^{s}
splitting the special vertex and
\delta_{split}^{o}
the other vertices.
Similarly, we write
\delta_{split}\Phi(\Gamma)=(\delta_{split}^{s}+\delta_{split}^{o})\Phi(\Gamma)
in
X_{g,n}
with
\delta_{split}^{s}
splitting the vertex that is the image of the special vertex, when the decoration on
\Gamma
is
\psi_{i}
, and
\delta_{split}^{o}
splitting the other vertices. (When the decoration on
\Gamma
is
E_{ij}
, we set
\delta_{split}^{s}\Phi(\Gamma)=0
.)
Since away from the special vertex the graph is not altered by
\Phi
we have

\Phi(\delta_{split}^{o}\Gamma)=\delta_{split}^{o}\Phi(\Gamma).

Keep in mind that if
\Gamma
has a
\psi_{j}
-decoration then
\Phi(\Gamma)
has one more structural edge than
\Gamma
, producing an additional
-
sign upon applying
\delta_{split}^{o}
. However, due to the sign
(-1)^{e}
in the definition of
\Phi
the signs on both sides of the above equation still agree.
Next, we then need to check that

(\delta_{split}^{s}+\delta_{join})\Phi(\Gamma)=\Phi((\delta_{split}^{s}+\delta_{res})\Gamma).

We consider cases according to the decoration at the special vertex of
\Gamma
.

First, suppose that the special vertex of
\Gamma
is decorated by
\delta_{0,A}
. Then we have
\Phi(\Gamma)=0
and
\delta_{res}\Gamma=0
, so we need to check that

\Phi(\delta_{split}^{s}\Gamma)=0.

The only terms of
\delta_{split}^{s}\Gamma
that do not themselves carry a
\delta
-decoration (and are hence sent to zero by
\Phi
) are those appearing in the last line of (
14
) on p.
14
. Both of these terms are mapped to the same graph via
\Phi
as depicted in (
32
), with opposite orderings of the two
\omega
-edges, and hence the matching terms cancel.

Next, suppose that the special vertex of
\Gamma
is decorated by
\psi_{i}
.
We have
\delta_{res}\Gamma=0
, and, since
\Phi(\Gamma)
has no
\epsilon
-legs,
\delta_{join}\Phi(\Gamma)=0
. We need to check that

\delta_{split}^{s}\Phi(\Gamma)=\Phi(\delta_{split}^{s}\Gamma).

Applying the definitions shows that both sides have the same form

Note that in all terms there is at least one
\epsilon
-leg.
Next we look at
\Phi(\Gamma)
. In this case
\delta_{split}^{s}\Phi(\Gamma)=0
, since
\Phi
removes the special vertex. Applying
\delta_{join}
to the right-hand side of (
31
) produces several graphs, by fusing a subset of
\epsilon
-legs together to produce a new
\epsilon
-leg, or fusing a subset of the
\epsilon
-legs to one
\omega
-leg.
The two cases in which all the
\epsilon
-hairs are fused to one
\omega
-leg precisely contribute (
34
). The cases where one or more
\epsilon
-legs remain contribute the terms (
35
).
To confirm the signs, note that in all cases considered the newly added edge is the first in the ordering.

Hence we conclude that

\delta_{join}\Phi(\Gamma)=\Phi(\delta_{split}^{s}\Gamma+\delta_{res}\Gamma),

as required.
∎

Proposition 5.5
.

The map
\Phi
is a surjective quasi-isomorphism with kernel generated by graphs in which the special vertex is decorated by some
\delta_{0,S}
, and by symmetric combinations of graphs with
\psi
-decorations on either half of some edge:

In either case,
\Phi(\widetilde{\Gamma})=\Gamma
.
Here we also use that at least one of the
\omega
-legs is adjacent to an internal vertex. Indeed, if this were not the case, then the graph would be either a single
(\omega,\omega)
-edge, or the union of an
(\omega,1)
-edge and an
(\omega,2)
-edge. In either case, we would have
2g+n<3
, which we have excluded from consideration.

The map takes graphs with decoration
\delta_{0,S}
to zero, and the orientation data ensures that symmetric combinations of
\psi
-decorations on paired half-edges also map to zero. Otherwise, distinct generators for
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}
map to distinct generators of
X_{g,n}
, so nothing else is in the kernel.

It remains to check that
J:=\ker\Phi
is acyclic. Decompose
J=J_{\delta}\oplus J_{\psi}
, where
J_{\delta}
and
J_{\psi}
are linear combinations of graphs with
\delta
- or
\psi
-decorations, respectively.

In these graphical depictions,
u
replaces a marked edge with a symmetric combination of
\psi
-decorations on its paired half-edges. This map gives a bijection between bases for
J_{\delta}
and for
J_{\psi}
, and is hence an isomorphism.
It then follows by Lemma
2.1
that
J
is acyclic, as required.
∎

Combining Propositions
5.3
and
5.5
gives the desired zig-zag of quasi-isomorphisms

\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}\leftarrow\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}\xrightarrow{\Phi}X_{g,n}.

6.
A quasi-isomorphic subcomplex

Although we do not fully understand the cohomology of
X_{g,n}
, we can describe many nontrivial classes.
We do so by identifying a quasi-isomorphic subcomplex
X^{\star}_{g,n}
and constructing an involution on
X^{\star}_{g,n}
that simplifies the differential. In this simplified subcomplex, we find direct summands whose cohomology we can either compute or bound from below.

6.1.
A quasi-isomorphic subcomplex

Recall that every connected component of a generator
\Gamma
for
X_{g,n}
contains an external vertex labeled by
\epsilon
or
\omega
.

Definition 6.1
.

A connected component that contains an
\omega
-decoration is an
\omega
-component
. All other connected components are
\epsilon
-components
.

Definition 6.2
.

Let
X^{\star}_{g,n}\subset X_{g,n}
be the subspace spanned by generators in which the union of all
\epsilon
-components contains no internal vertices and at most one decoration from
\{1,\dots,n\}
.

In other words, if
\Gamma
is a generator for
X^{\star}_{g,n}
, then the union of its
\epsilon
-components is either empty or consists of an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge, an
(\epsilon,j)
-edge, or one of each. Here are two examples:

Lemma 6.3
.

The graded subspace
X^{\star}_{g,n}\subset X_{g,n}
is a subcomplex.

Proof.

Let
\Gamma
be a generator for
X^{\star}_{g,n}
. The differential is a sum of two parts
\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}
. The part
\delta_{split}
acts separately on the internal vertices of each connected component. It cannot create internal vertices in a component that does not already have any, and it does change the decorations. So
\delta_{split}\Gamma
is a linear combination of generators for
X^{\star}_{g,n}
.

Now consider the terms that appear in
\delta_{join}\Gamma
, which are obtained by joining external vertices of one or several components. If at least one of the joined components is an
\omega
-component, then the resulting graph is a generator for
X^{\star}_{g,n}
. However, if all components that are joined are
\epsilon
-components, then the resulting graph has either a loop or two
\epsilon
-labeled external vertices adjacent to the same internal vertex, and hence is zero in
X_{g,n}
.
∎

Proposition 6.4
.

The inclusion
X^{\star}_{g,n}\subset X_{g,n}
is a quasi-isomorphism.

Proof.

Filter the complexes
X^{\star}_{g,n}
and
X_{g,n}
by the number of internal vertices in
\omega
-components.
We claim that the inclusion induces a quasi-isomorphism between the associated graded complexes with respect to this filtration.

The associated graded complexes have differential
\delta_{join}^{\epsilon,\epsilon}+\delta_{split}^{\epsilon}
, with
\delta_{join}^{\epsilon,\epsilon}
the part of
\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}
(as defined in the proof of Lemma
6.3
) that joins
\epsilon
-legs of
\epsilon
-components only and
\delta_{split}^{\epsilon}
the part of
\delta_{split}
that splits vertices in
\epsilon
-components only. Note that the differential on
X^{\star}_{g,n}
is 0.
Furthermore, we have the direct sum decomposition

(X_{g,n},\delta_{join}^{\epsilon,\epsilon}+\delta_{split}^{\epsilon})=X^{\star}_{g,n}\oplus(W,\delta_{join}^{\epsilon,\epsilon}+\delta_{split}^{\epsilon}),

with
W\subset X_{g,n}
spanned by graphs that are not generators for
X^{\star}_{g,n}
.
Generators of
W
are graphs in which the
\epsilon
-components contain an internal vertex or more than one leg labelled
1,\dots,n
.
We further decompose

W=W^{\prime}\oplus W^{\prime\prime},

where
W^{\prime}
is spanned by graphs that do not contain an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge, and
W^{\prime\prime}
is spanned by those that do.
Note that
W^{\prime\prime}
is isomorphic (up to degree shift) to the
W^{\prime}
summand that arises in
X_{g-1,n}
, so it suffices to show that
W^{\prime}
is acyclic.
To this end consider the decomposition of graded vector spaces

This is map is injective; it has a one-sided inverse obtained by removing both new vertices and the edge between them, and adding an external vertex labeled
\epsilon
to each of the dangling edges.
This map is also surjective, since the unique
\epsilon
-decoration in an
\epsilon
-component of a graph in
W_{1}^{\prime}
must be adjacent to an internal vertex.
(If it was adjacent to an
j
-decorated leg the graph would not be in
W
, and
(\epsilon,\omega)
-edges are forbidden in
X_{g,n}
.)
∎

We note that in the above proof the presence of the part of the differential
\delta_{join}^{\omega}
played no role. The same proof also shows the following auxiliary result, which we will use in the proof of Proposition
7.2
.

Lemma 6.5
.

The inclusion
(X^{\star}_{g},\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}+\delta_{split})\to(X_{g},\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}+\delta_{split})
is a quasi-isomorphism of dg vector spaces.

6.2.
A simplifying involution

We now construct an involution of
X^{\star}_{g,n}
that simplifies the differential. This involution is given by reattaching subsets of the
\epsilon
-decorated external vertices in all possible ways and motivates the introduction of the subcomplex
X^{\star}_{g,n}
; see Remark
6.6
.

Remark 6.6
.

The restriction on the union of all
\epsilon
-components of graphs in
X^{\star}_{g,n}
(Definition
6.2
) guarantees that the reattachment operation does not produce connected components without any
\epsilon
- or
\omega
-decoration. For this reason,
R_{S}
is well-defined on
X^{\star}_{g,n}
. It is not well-defined on
X_{g,n}
.

We now consider the graded endomorphism
\Xi
of
X^{\star}_{g,n}
, given by

\Xi(\Gamma)=(-1)^{\#\epsilon}\sum_{S}R_{S}(\Gamma),

where the sum runs over all subsets of the set of
\epsilon
-decorations, and
\#\epsilon
is the number of
\epsilon
-decorations in
\Gamma
.

Lemma 6.7
.

The map
\Xi
is an involution, i.e., it is invertible and
\Xi^{-1}=\Xi
.

Proof.

Any graph appearing in
\Xi\circ\Xi\,(\Gamma)
is obtained by reattaching some subset
S
of the
\epsilon
-decorated legs to internal vertices. Each such graph appears
2^{|S|}
different ways, with signs that cancel unless
S=\emptyset
.
∎

a graph,

a non-empty subset of its
\epsilon
-decorated external vertices and
j=1,\dots,n

This operation creates precisely one new structural edge, which we take to be first in the ordering, preserving the relative ordering of the remaining edges.
Note that the operation also makes sense if applied not to a numbered leg, but an
\omega
-labeled leg, and we shall denote the sum of such operations applied to the two
\omega
-legs by
R_{S}^{\omega}
.

We also define

\tilde{\delta}_{join}^{j}(\Gamma)=\sum_{|S|\geq 1}|\,S|\cdot R_{S}^{j}(\Gamma),

where the sum runs over all non-empty subsets of the set of
\epsilon
-legs of
\Gamma
.
We then have the following result:

Proposition 6.8
.

Let

\tilde{\delta}:=\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\tilde{\delta}_{join}^{j}

Then
\tilde{\delta}=\Xi\circ\delta\circ\Xi
.
In particular,
\Xi
defines an isomorphism of dg vector spaces

\Xi\colon(X^{\star}_{g,n},\tilde{\delta})\to(X^{\star}_{g,n},\delta).

Proof.

The proof is similar to that of
[
36
, Lemma 3.6]
; the argument there goes through essentially unchanged, even though the complexes
X^{\star}_{g,n}
we consider here are different. We give only a condensed sketch of the proof.

We introduce the following notation. For
S
a subset of the
\epsilon
-legs in some graph
\Gamma\in X^{\star}_{g,n}
we denote by
R_{S}^{\epsilon}(\Gamma)
the graph obtained by reattaching the legs in
S
to a new
\epsilon
-decorated vertex.

Using the fact that
\Xi^{-1}=\Xi
, one computes that

(\Xi\circ\delta_{split}\circ\Xi)(\Gamma)=\delta_{split}(\Gamma)+\sum_{|S|\geq 2}|S|\cdot R_{S}^{\epsilon}(\Gamma)+\sum_{|S|\geq 2}(|S|-1)\cdot R^{\prime}_{S}(\Gamma)+\sum_{|S|\geq 1}\sum_{j\in\{1,\dots,n,\omega\}}R_{S}^{j}(\Gamma),

Here
S
runs over subsets of the set of
\epsilon
-legs.
Similarly, one may compute

(\Xi\circ\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}\circ\Xi)(\Gamma)=\sum_{|S|\geq 2}(1-|S|)\cdot R_{S}^{\epsilon}(\Gamma)+\sum_{|S|\geq 2}(1-|S|)\cdot R^{\prime}_{S}(\Gamma).

Together we find that

\displaystyle(\Xi\circ(\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon})\circ\Xi)(\Gamma)

\displaystyle=(\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}+\delta_{join}^{\omega})\Gamma+\sum_{|S|\geq 1}\sum_{j\in\{1,\dots,n\}}R_{S}^{j}(\Gamma)

\displaystyle=\delta(\Gamma)+\sum_{|S|\geq 1}\sum_{j\in\{1,\dots,n\}}R_{S}^{j}(\Gamma).

Then one may finally compute that

\Big(\Xi\circ\sum_{|S|\geq 1}R_{S}^{j}\circ\Xi\Big)\,(\Gamma)=\sum_{|S|\geq 1}|S|\cdot R_{S}^{j}(\Gamma)=\tilde{\delta}_{join}^{j}(\Gamma).

Putting the above computations together we find that

\displaystyle\Xi\circ\tilde{\delta}\circ\Xi

\displaystyle=\Xi\circ\Big(\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}-\sum_{j}\tilde{\delta}_{join}^{j}\Big)\circ\Xi=\delta+\sum_{j}\delta_{join}^{j}-\sum_{j}\delta_{join}^{j}=\delta,

which proves the proposition.
∎

7.
The weight 2 compactly supported cohomology of
{\mathcal{M}}_{g}

We now focus on the special case where
n=0
. Using the quasi-isomorphic subcomplex
X^{\star}_{g}\subset X_{g}
, with its simplified differential
\tilde{\delta}
, we shall see that the cohomology of
X_{g}
can be fully expressed through the cohomology of the ordinary commutative graph complexes
G^{(g^{\prime},n^{\prime})}
of Section
4.1
, with
n^{\prime}=1,2
and
g^{\prime}=g,g-1,g-2
.

When
n=0
, the differential
\tilde{\delta}
in Proposition
6.8
further simplifies to

\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}
.
We define the subcomplex

(36)

H_{g}\subset(X^{\star}_{g},\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon})

spanned by graphs with either no
\epsilon
-decorations, or exactly two on an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge. Note that
\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}
vanishes on
H_{g}
.

We also introduce the space

G^{(\bullet,n)}=\bigoplus_{g}G^{(g,n)},

that inherits an additional grading by the genus.
We also define the exterior product

\mathbb{W}_{\bullet}=\bigwedge^{2}G^{(\bullet,1)}

This comes with a grading inherited from the genus grading; let
\mathbb{W}_{g}
be the homogeneous part of genus
g
.

Lemma 7.1
.

The subspace
H_{g}

is a subcomplex with respect to
\tilde{\delta}=\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}
, and
(H_{g},\tilde{\delta})
is isomorphic to

\mathbb{W}_{g}[-3]\oplus G^{(g-1,2)}_{as}[-3]\oplus\mathbb{W}_{g-1}[-4]\oplus G^{(g-2,2)}_{as}[-4].

Here the subscript
(-)_{as}
refers to taking the antisymmetric part under the
\mathbb{S}_{2}
-action permuting the labels
1,2
.

Proof.

Graphs in
H_{g}
have exactly two
\omega
-decorated legs, and every connected component has an
\omega
- or
\epsilon
-decorated leg. There are four possibilities, with and without an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge, and with 1 or 2
\omega
-components:

6.5
.
It hence suffices to show that the diagonal inclusion

(H_{g},\delta_{split})\to(X_{g},\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon})

is a quasi-isomorphism.
Each complex splits, as in the proof of Proposition
6.4
,
into one piece generated by graphs that do not have any
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge and a complementary piece spanned by those that do. So, we write
H^{\prime}_{g}
and
X^{\prime}_{g}
for the subcomplexes of
H_{g}
and
X_{g}
, respectively, spanned by graphs that do not have any
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge. Similarly, we write
H^{\prime\prime}_{g}
and
X^{\prime\prime}_{g}
for the subcomplexes spanned by graphs with an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge. We then have

\displaystyle H_{g}

\displaystyle\cong H_{g}^{\prime}\oplus H_{g}^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle X_{g}

\displaystyle\cong X_{g}^{\prime}\oplus X_{g}^{\prime\prime}.

Note that
H_{g}^{\prime\prime}\cong H_{g-1}^{\prime}[-1]
and
X_{g}^{\prime\prime}\cong X_{g-1}^{\prime}[-1]
, so
it suffices to show that
H_{g}^{\prime}\subset X^{\prime}_{g}
is a quasi-isomorphism.

We furthermore have a direct sum decomposition of complexes

(X_{g}^{\prime},\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon})\cong(H_{g}^{\prime},\delta_{split})\oplus(U,\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon}),

where
U\subset X_{g}^{\prime}
is the subcomplex spanned by graphs with at least one
\epsilon
-leg.

U
is acyclic.

Proof of Theorem
1.2
.

By Propositions
6.4
,
6.8
, and
7.2
, the composition

H_{g}\hookrightarrow(X^{\star}_{g},\delta_{split}+\delta_{join}^{\epsilon})\xrightarrow{\Phi}(X^{\star}_{g},\delta_{split}+\delta_{join})\hookrightarrow X_{g}

is a quasi-isomorphism. The cohomology of the right-hand side is
\gr^{2}H_{c}^{\bullet}({\mathcal{M}}_{g})
. The cohomology of
H_{g}
is expressed via Lemma
7.1
through the cohomology of the complexes
G^{(g^{\prime},n^{\prime})}
that compute
\gr^{0}H_{c}^{\bullet}({\mathcal{M}}_{g^{\prime},n^{\prime}})
by Theorem
4.1
, and Theorem
1.2
follows.
∎

8.
Direct summands with marked points

Let
\Gamma
be a generator for
X^{\star}_{g,n}
, and let us now assume
n\geq 1
. Recall that each such generator has some number of
\epsilon
-decorations and precisely two
\omega
-decorations. The remaining external vertices are decorated by a bijection to
\{1,\ldots,n\}
. Each component has at least one decoration from
\{\epsilon,\omega\}
.

Definition 8.1
.

A connected component of
\Gamma
is
isolated
if it contains no decorations from
\{1,\ldots,n,\epsilon\}
.

In other words, a component is isolated if all of its external vertices are decorated with
\omega
. Components that do have a decoration from
\{1,\ldots,n,\epsilon\}
are
non-isolated
. We decompose
X^{\star}_{g,n}
according to the number of
\omega
decorations that are contained non-isolated components.

Definition 8.2
.

Let
H_{g,n}
,
J_{g,n}
, and
K_{g,n}
be the graded subspaces of
X^{\star}_{g,n}
spanned by graphs with
0
,
1
, or
2
of their
\omega
-decorations contained in non-isolated components, respectively.

No term of the differential
\tilde{\delta}
can make an isolated connected component into a non-isolated one or vice versa, so
we have a direct sum decomposition of dg vector spaces

(37)

(X^{\star}_{g,n},\tilde{\delta})=H_{g,n}\oplus J_{g,n}\oplus K_{g,n}.

We will study the cohomology of the summands separately. Unfortunately, we have nothing to say about
H(K_{g,n})
.

8.1.
The cohomology of
H_{g,n}

The summand
H_{g,n}
contributes to the cohomology of
X^{\star}_{g,n}
only when
n=1
, and that contribution is well-understood.

Lemma 8.3
.

We have
H_{g,1}\cong H_{g}
and
H_{g,n}=0
for
n\geq 2
.

Proof.

By the definition of
X^{\star}_{g,n}
, the non-isolated components that do not contain
\omega
-decorations consist of either an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge, an
(\epsilon,j)
-edge, or one of each. If
n\geq 2
, then none of the generators for
X^{\star}_{g,n}
are in
H_{g,n}
. Moreover, the generators for
H_{g,1}
are precisely the graphs of the form

The differential acts by
\delta_{split}
on the isolated component, so
J_{g,n}
decomposes as a direct sum of subcomplexes determined by the genus of the isolated component. The subcomplex where the non-isolated part has genus
h
can be written as a tensor product
J^{\star}_{h,n}\otimes G^{(h^{\prime},1)}[-1]
, where
h+h^{\prime}=g
and
J^{\star}_{h,n}
is a graph complex perfectly analogous to
X^{\star}_{h,n}
, except that each generator has exactly one
\omega
decoration instead of two, and this
\omega
-decoration must be part of a non-isolated component.
1
1

1

The latter condition is automatically satisfied if
n\geq 2
.

We then have a decomposition

(38)

J_{g,n}=\bigoplus_{h+h^{\prime}=g}J^{\star}_{h,n}\otimes G^{(h^{\prime},1)}[-1].

The degree shift on the factor
G^{(h^{\prime},1)}
is due to the additional structural edge that contains the
\omega
decoration.
The degree of a generator for
J^{\star}_{h,n}
is the number of structural edges plus one, just as for
X_{g^{\prime},n}
. The cohomology of
J^{\star}_{h,n}
is difficult to evaluate when
h
is large; we leave its study for
h\geq 2
to future work. Theorems
1.6
and
1.7
use only the cohomology of
J^{\star}_{0,n}
and
J^{\star}_{1,n}
, which we now describe.

8.3.
The cohomology of
J^{\star}_{0,n}

We now explain how the cohomology of
J^{\star}_{0,n}
is closely related to
W_{0}H^{\bullet}_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})
and
W_{0}H^{\bullet}_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1})
. Let
V_{1}\subset J^{*}_{0,n}
be the subcomplex generated by graphs with no
\epsilon
decorations. Each generator for
V_{1}
is a rooted tree with
n
leaves labeled
\{1,\ldots,n\}
and a root labeled
\omega
. Let
V_{0}
be the complementary graded subspace generated by graphs with an
\epsilon
-decoration. Since the genus is zero, there are no
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edges, and no connected component can have both an
\epsilon
-decoration and also an
\omega
-decoration. So each generator for
V_{0}
has two connected components, an
(\epsilon,j)
-edge and an
\omega
-rooted tree with
(n-1)
leaves labeled
\{1,\ldots,\hat{\jmath},\ldots n\}

where the internal arrows on
V_{0}
and
V_{1}
are
\delta_{split}
. Note that
V_{1}\cong G^{(0,n+1)}[-2]
, and
(V_{0},\delta_{split})\cong\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}G^{(0,n)}[-2]
. Therefore
H(V_{1})\cong W_{0}H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1})[-2]
has dimension
(n-1)!
, supported in degree
n
, and
H(V_{0},\delta_{split})
has dimension
n(n-2)!
, supported in degree
n-1
. By Lemma
2.1
(
1
), the first statement of Proposition
8.4
follows if we can show that

\delta_{join}\colon H(V_{0},\delta_{split})\to H(V_{1})

is surjective. For
1\leq j\leq n
, let
D_{j}\subset{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1}
be the locally closed divisor parametrizing 1-nodal curves where
j
and
\omega
collide. Then
D_{j}\cong{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}
, the union
{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1}\sqcup\Big(\bigsqcup_{j}D_{j}\Big)
is open in
\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{0,n+1}
, and
\bigsqcup_{j}D_{j}
is closed in this union. Then
\delta_{join}
is naturally identified with the excision coboundary map

\delta\colon\bigoplus_{j}W_{0}H^{\bullet}_{c}(D_{j})\to W_{0}H^{\bullet+1}_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1}).

We must show that
\delta
is surjective. We will give a short algebraic proof of this surjectivity.

To this end, it will be convenient to work with the
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-modules

\tilde{J}^{\star}_{0,n}:=J^{\star}_{0,n}\otimes\sgn_{n}.

Tensoring with
\sgn_{n}
can be nicely incorporated in the sign conventions on graph complexes; we take generators for
\tilde{J}^{\star}_{0,n}
to be graphs with a total ordering of all edges (not just the structural edges), and impose the relation that permuting the edges induces multiplication by the sign of the permutation. Decompose
\tilde{J}^{\star}_{0,n}\cong\tilde{V}_{0}\oplus\tilde{V}_{1}
, as above.

Then we can identify the cohomology groups with subspaces of free Lie algebras

\displaystyle H(\tilde{V}_{0},\tilde{\delta}_{split})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})[-n]

\displaystyle H(\tilde{V}_{1})

\displaystyle=\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})[-n-1]

with
\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})
the part of the free Lie algebra with generators
x_{1},\dots,x_{n}
for which each generator appears exactly once. Here the identification between (trivalent) trees and Lie words is such that the root of our tree is taken to be
\omega
, every vertex is replaced by one Lie bracket, and the
j
-labeled leaf is replaced by
x_{j}
, e.g.

The differential is then given by

(39)

(F_{1},\dots,F_{n})\to\sum_{j=1}^{n}[x_{j},F_{j}],

which is surjective, as required.

For the second statement of Proposition
8.4
we take for granted the well-known fact that
H_{c}^{n-3}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})\cong\mathsf{Lie}((n))\otimes\sgn_{n}
.
It then remains to check that the kernel of (
39
) can be identified with
\mathsf{Lie}((n))
as an
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-module.
We may do this by providng an injective map

\iota:\mathsf{Lie}((n))\to\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})

whose image is in the kernel of (
39
).
To construct
\iota
, we use the following notation
for elements of
\mathsf{Lie}((n))
.
We have that
\mathsf{Lie}((n))\cong\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1})

and we write

f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}):=\langle f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}),x_{n}\rangle\in\mathsf{Lie}((n))

for the element corresponding to a Lie expression
f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1})\in\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1})
.
The
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-action on
\mathsf{Lie}((n))
is defined by permuting variables, considering
\langle-,-\rangle
formally as an invariant inner product.
In particular, for each
j
we have Lie expressions

f_{j}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})\in\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})
such that

f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\langle f_{j}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n}),x_{j}\rangle.

We then define the map
\iota
such that

\iota(f):=(f_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{n})\in\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n}).

It is clear that
\iota
is an injection since
f
may be recovered from any of the
f_{j}
.

We are hence left with checking that the composition of
\iota
and (
39
) is zero.
To this end, note that in
\mathsf{Lie}((n+1))
we have the equality

\displaystyle\langle[x_{j},f_{j}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})],x_{n+1}\rangle

\displaystyle=-\langle f_{j}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n}),[x_{j},x_{n+1}]\rangle

\displaystyle=f(x_{1},\dots,[x_{n+1},x_{j}],\dots,x_{n})

\displaystyle=\langle f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,[x_{n+1},x_{j}],\dots,x_{n-1}),x_{n}\rangle,

for
j=1,\dots,n-1
, using invariance of our formal inner product
\langle-,-\rangle
and the definition of the
f_{j}
.
Thus in
\mathsf{Lie}((n+1))
we have that

\displaystyle\langle\sum_{j=1}^{n}[x_{j},f_{j}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})],x_{n+1}\rangle

\displaystyle=\langle-[x_{n+1},f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1})]+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,[x_{n+1},x_{j}],\dots,x_{n-1}),x_{n}\rangle=0

by the Jacobi identity.
Hence
\sum_{j=1}^{n}[x_{j},f_{j}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})]=0
as desired and the second statement of Proposition
8.4
follows.

∎

The second statement of Proposition
8.4
was kindly pointed out to us by the anonymous referee, whom we thank for her or his contribution.

8.4.
The cohomology of
J^{\star}_{1,n}

Each generator for
J^{\star}_{1,n}
has one of six combinatorial types: with or without an
(\epsilon,j)
-edge, and with 0, 1, or 2 other
\epsilon
-decorations. The following diagram depicts one generator of each type (for varying values of
n
). We denote the corresponding graded subspaces of
J^{\star}_{1,n}
by
V_{i,k}
, as shown. The notation is chosen so that a generator for
V_{i,k}
has
1-k
edges of type
(\epsilon,j)
and
2-i

Let us filter
J^{\ast}_{1,n}
by the number of
\epsilon
-decorations and consider the associated spectral sequence. On the
E_{0}
-page (the associated graded), the differential is
\delta_{split}
, which preserves each of the six combinatorial types. So
E_{1}
is the direct sum of the homologies of the associated graph complexes, with respect to
\delta_{split}
. Each term then has an evident interpretation in terms of weight zero cohomology of moduli spaces; for instance

H(V_{1,0})\cong\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}W_{0}H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1})[-3]\quad\quad\mbox{ and }\quad\quad H(V_{2,1})\cong W_{0}H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{1,n+1})[-2].

Note that the cohomology of
V_{i,k}
is supported in degree
n+i+k
.

The differential on
E_{1}
is the part of
\delta_{join}
that reduces the number of
\epsilon
-decorations by exactly 1. This further decomposes as two parts, one that eliminates an
(\epsilon,j)
-edge, and one that decreases the number of other
\epsilon
-decorations by
1
. Therefore, the
E_{1}
-page is the total complex of a diagram of the following form:

(40)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W_{0}H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1})[-3]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W_{0}H_{c}{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+2}[-3]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W_{0}H_{c}{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n+1}[-2]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}W_{0}H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n})[-3]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}W_{0}H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{0,n+1})[-3]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}W_{0}H_{c}{\mathcal{M}}_{1,n}[-2].}

The arrows are once again coboundary maps in excision sequences arising from stratifications of moduli spaces.

As in our computation of
H(J^{\star}_{0,n})
, we find it helpful to tensor once again with
\sgn_{n}
and then give an algebraic interpretation for the resulting diagram. Let
\tilde{J}^{\star}_{1,n}:=J^{\star}_{1,n}\otimes\sgn_{n}
, with differential
\tilde{\delta}=\tilde{\delta}_{split}+\tilde{\delta}_{join}
. Similarly, let
\tilde{V}_{i,k}:=V_{i,k}\otimes\sgn_{n}
. Recall that tensoring with
\sgn_{n}
amounts to equipping each generator with a total ordering of all of its edges, not just the structural edges, and imposing the usual relation that reordering the edges is multiplication by the sign of the induced permutation. We then have

\displaystyle H(\tilde{V}_{0,1},\tilde{\delta}_{split})

\displaystyle\cong\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})[-n-1]

(41)

\displaystyle H(\tilde{V}_{1,1},\tilde{\delta}_{split})

\displaystyle\cong\mathsf{Assoc}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})[-n-2]

(42)

\displaystyle H(\tilde{V}_{2,1},\tilde{\delta}_{split})

\displaystyle\cong\mathsf{Assoc}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}[-n-3].

Here,
\mathsf{Assoc}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})
is the subspace of the free associative algebra spanned by words in which each variable appears exactly once, and
\mathbb{S}_{2}
acts by reversing each word (corresponding to the symmetry reversing the orientation of a based loop).
Under the identification (
41
), the associative word
x_{1}\cdots x_{n}
corresponds to the graph

that appears in an

, i.e.,

, and so on.

With these identifications, the

The bottom left space is concentrated in degree
n
, and each arrow increases the degree by one.

(43)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{Assoc}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})}

Each vertical arrow in (
43
) is defined by the formula

(44)

(F_{1},\dots,F_{n})\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{n}[x_{j},F_{j}].

The horizontal arrows are the canonical inclusions and projections, so that the cohomology of each row of (
43
) is concentrated in the middle term. It is hence easy to check (for example, using Lemma
2.1
again) that the total complex of (
43
) is quasi-isomorphic to the two-term complex built from its row-wise cohomology.
It hence remains to study these middle cohomology groups of each row, and the induced map between them.

To this end let
{\mathsf{Pois}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})
be the part of the free Poisson algebra in
x_{1},\dots,x_{n}
in which each
x_{j}
appears exactly once.
Its elements are linear combinations of Poisson expressions of the form

F(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=f_{1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\wedge\cdots\wedge f_{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}),

where the
f_{j}
are Lie words, such that each variable
x_{j}
appears exactly once in
F
. Let
{\mathsf{Pois}}^{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})
be the subspace spanned by expressions that are products of exactly
k
Lie words. There is a natural map

(45)

D_{n}^{k}:\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}{\mathsf{Pois}}^{k}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})\to{\mathsf{Pois}}^{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}),

given again by the expression (
44
), i.e.,

(F_{1},\dots,F_{n})\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{n}[x_{j},F_{j}].
. Let us define

\displaystyle\mathbb{A}_{n}^{k}

\displaystyle:=\ker D_{n}^{k}

\displaystyle\mathbb{B}_{n}^{k}:=\coker D_{n}^{k},

and

(46)

\displaystyle\mathbb{A}_{n}

\displaystyle:=\bigoplus_{j\geq 1}\mathbb{A}_{n}^{2j+1}

\displaystyle\mathbb{B}_{n}:=\bigoplus_{j\geq 1}\mathbb{B}_{n}^{2j+1}.

All objects here are naturally
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-representations, by changing the variable indices and order of summands on the left-hand side of (
45
). For example, we have
\mathbb{A}_{1}=\mathbb{B}_{1}=\mathbb{A}_{2}=\mathbb{B}_{2}=\mathbb{A}_{3}=0
,
\mathbb{B}_{3}
and
\mathbb{A}_{4}
are one-dimensional trivial representations, and
\mathbb{B}_{4}
is a three-dimensional irreducible representation of
\mathbb{S}_{4}
.

Proposition 8.6
.

We have
J^{\star}_{1,0}=0
. For
n\geq 1
we have an isomorphism of graded
\mathbb{S}_{n}
-modules

H(J^{\star}_{1,n},\delta)\cong(\mathbb{A}_{n}[-n-1]\oplus\mathbb{B}_{n}[-n-2])\otimes\sgn_{n}.

Equivalently, we must show that
H(\tilde{J}^{\star}_{1,n},\tilde{\delta})\cong\mathbb{A}_{n}[-n-1]\oplus\mathbb{B}_{n}[-n-2]

we get the diagram

The cohomology of (

) is the kernel plus the cokernel of the differential

, i.e., the direct sum of

The above description of the spaces
\mathbb{A}_{n}
and
\mathbb{B}_{n}
is not very explicit.
However, we can at least provide the following lower bound on the dimensions.

Lemma 8.7
.

For
n\geq 3
we have

\dim\mathbb{B}_{n}\geq(n-2)!.

Proof.

From the definition of
\mathbb{B}_{n}
, we have

\dim\mathbb{B}_{n}\geq\dim\left(\bigoplus_{k\geq 1}{\mathsf{Pois}}^{2k+1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\right)-\dim\left(\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\bigoplus_{k\geq 1}{\mathsf{Pois}}^{2k+1}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})\right).

From the top row of (
43
), we have

\displaystyle\dim\left(\bigoplus_{k\geq 1}{\mathsf{Pois}}^{2k+1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\right)

\displaystyle=\dim\left(\mathsf{Assoc}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\right)-\dim\left(\mathsf{Assoc}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}\right)-\dim\left(\mathsf{Lie}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\right)

\displaystyle=n!-\frac{n!}{2}-(n-1)!,

which simplifies to
\frac{1}{2}(n-2)(n-1)!
Here, we have used that the action of
\mathbb{S}_{2}
on associative words of length
\geq 2
is faithful in computing
\dim\left(\mathsf{Assoc}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})_{\mathbb{S}_{2}}\right)=\frac{n!}{2}
.
By the same computation (valid for
n\geq 3
) we also see that

\displaystyle\dim\left(\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\bigoplus_{k\geq 1}{\mathsf{Pois}}^{2k+1}(x_{1},\dots,\hat{x}_{j},\dots,x_{n})\right)=\frac{1}{2}n(n-3)(n-2)!

Hence

\dim\mathbb{B}_{n}\geq\frac{1}{2}\left((n-2)(n-1)-n(n-3)\right)(n-2)!,

which is
(n-2)!
, as required.
∎

-class is of pure weight 2 in
H^{2}(\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{g,1})
and is represented by a smooth and closed differential form
\eta
without logarithmic poles. The cup product
\psi\cup\colon\gr_{\bullet}H_{c}^{\bullet}({\mathcal{M}}_{g,1})\to\gr_{\bullet+2}H_{c}^{\bullet+2}({\mathcal{M}}_{g,1})
is therefore induced by the action of
\eta
on currents, which also induces a compatible action on every term on every page in our weight spectral sequence. The
\xi_{\Gamma}
-pullback of
\psi
is the corresponding
\psi
-class on
\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{\Gamma}
, and it follows that
\psi\cup
is induced by multiplication by
\psi
on every term of
\mathsf{GK}_{g,1}
. The claim follows by descending from
\mathsf{GK}^{2}_{g,1}
to
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{2}_{g,1}
and then lifting to
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}^{2}_{g,1}
. This finishes the proof of Theorem
1.6
.

To show Theorem
1.7
we consider again the injection from (
49
) to
\gr_{2}H_{c}^{\bullet}({\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
, for
n\geq 2
.
Then Proposition
8.4
directly produces the first summand in the formula of Theorem
1.7
, and Lemma
8.6
produces the second summand.
The assertion on the dimension of
\mathbb{B}_{n}
is shown in Lemma
8.7
.
∎

Remark 8.8
.

Proposition
8.6
yields an additional summand to
\gr_{2}H^{\bullet}_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})
corresponding to the subspace

(\mathbb{A}_{n}[-n-1]\otimes\sgn_{n})\subset H(J^{\star}_{1,n}).

Lacking lower bounds on the dimension of
\mathbb{A}_{n}
, we omitted this summand from the statement of Theorem
1.7
.

.)
The corresponding cocycle in
(X^{\star}_{3,2},\delta)
is obtained by applying the involution

]
, we know that

H(J^{\star}_{0,2})\otimes H(G^{(3,1)})[-1]

Appendix A
A direct map
X_{g,n}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}

We have connected the complexes
X_{g,n}
and
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
through a zig-zag of quasi-isomorphisms. Here, we construct a direct map

F\colon X_{g,n}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}

that fits into a homotopy commutative triangle with the maps in the zig-zag.

The map
F
is useful for giving geometrically meaningful representatives in
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
of the cohomology classes we have constructed in
X_{g,n}
. By Theorem
3.3
, for
(g,n)\neq(1,1)
, the projection
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{2}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
is a quasi-isomorphism. Hence each cocycle in
\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
lifts to a cocycle on
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}^{2}
, uniquely up to exact terms. We now turn to the construction of the map
F
, which we define initially as a map of graded vector spaces.

Let
\Gamma
be a generator for
X_{g,n}
with
e
structural edges.
First, suppose
\Gamma
has no
\epsilon
-decorations. At least one of the
\omega
-decorations must be adjacent to an internal vertex. If both
\omega
-decorations are adjacent to internal vertices, then
F(\gamma)
is obtained by joining the
\omega
-legs to form a new edge, and decorating either half-edge by
\psi_{i}
, in the antisymmetric linear combination:

(50)

It remains to consider the cases where
\Gamma
has a positive number of
\epsilon
-decorations. First, suppose both of the
\omega
-decorations are adjacent to internal vertices. By the orientation relations, we may assume these internal vertices are distinct. Call them
v
and
v^{\prime}
. Then let
\Gamma_{v}
be the graph formed by making
v
the special vertex, attaching all
\epsilon
- and
\omega
-decorated legs to that vertex and decorating it by
\delta_{0,S}
with
S
the union of the half-edges adjacent to the
\epsilon
-decorations and the half-edge towards
v^{\prime}
.
Then
F(\Gamma)=\frac{1}{2}(\Gamma_{v}-\Gamma_{v^{\prime}})
. Pictorially:

Proposition A.1
.

The map
F\colon X_{g,n}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
is a map of complexes and fits into a homotopy commutative triangle

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{g,n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}

Proof.

We begin by constructing a degree
-1
map of graded vector spaces

h\colon\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2},

and show that it satisfies the required equation (
52
) to give a chain homotopy from
F\circ\Phi
to
\pi
. We will then use
h
to show that
F
is a map of complexes, and thereby prove the proposition.

Let
\Gamma
be a generator for
\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}^{2}
. We define
h(\Gamma)
by a local replacement at the special vertex as follows.

\Gamma
is decorated by

is not joined to a leg, so the half-edge is joined to a half-edge at an internal vertex

be the graph obtained by merging the special vertex with
v

F\circ\Phi
to
\pi

(52)

F(\Phi(\Gamma))-\pi(\Gamma)=\delta h(\Gamma)+h(\delta(\Gamma)).

\Gamma

Finally, suppose the special vertex of
\Gamma
is decorated by
E_{ij}
, with
i,j
half-edges incident to the special vertex. Then
\pi(\Gamma)=0
and
h(\Gamma)=0
. We must show that
F(\Phi(\Gamma))=h(\delta\Gamma)
, and we consider cases according to whether
i
and
j
are joined to legs. If both are joined to legs, then
F(\Phi(\Gamma))=h(\delta\Gamma)=0
. If only
j
is joined to a leg, then one computes, with
e
the number of structural edges of

This completes the proof of (
52
).

Having proved (
52
), we have that for all
\Gamma\in\widetilde{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}

\delta F(\Phi(\Gamma))-F(\delta\Phi(\Gamma))=0.

By Proposition
5.5
, the map
\Phi
is surjective, and hence
\delta\circ F=F\circ\delta
. We conclude that
F
is a map of chain complexes, and
h
is chain homotopy from
F\circ\Phi
to
\pi
, as required.
∎

A.1.
The pullback map

Recall that the projection
\pi\colon{\mathcal{M}}_{g,1}\to{\mathcal{M}}_{g}
is proper and extends to a morphism on the stable curves compactifications, also denoted
\pi\colon\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{g,1}\to\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{g}
. Recall also that the boundary divisors
\partial{\mathcal{M}}_{g,1}:=\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{g,1}\smallsetminus{\mathcal{M}}_{g,1}
and
\partial{\mathcal{M}}_{g}:=\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{g}\smallsetminus{\mathcal{M}}_{g}
have normal crossings. Applying the “fundamental simplicial constructions” as in
[
14
, §
II
.I]
gives an induced morphism
\pi^{*}
from the simplicial resolution of the constant sheaf
\mathbb{Q}
on
\partial{\mathcal{M}}_{g}
to that of the constant sheaf
\mathbb{Q}
on
\partial{\mathcal{M}}_{g,1}
, induced by the normal crossings structure. After realizing the compactly supported cohomology of
{\mathcal{M}}_{g,1}
and of
{\mathcal{M}}_{g}
as the reduced cohomology of the mapping cones for the inclusions
\partial{\mathcal{M}}_{g,1}\to\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{g,1}
and
\partial{\mathcal{M}}_{g}\to\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{g}
, respectively, we get an induced pullback morphism between the weight spectral sequences that abuts to
\pi^{*}\colon\gr H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{g})\to\gr H_{c}({\mathcal{M}}_{g,1})
.

We consider the graphical interpretation of the the induced map on the
E_{1}
-page of the weight spectral sequence, i.e., the induced map between the Getzler-Kapranov graph complexes. We claim that

\pi^{*}\colon\mathsf{GK}_{g,0}\to\mathsf{GK}_{g,1}

is given by the formula

(53)

\pi^{*}\Gamma=\sum_{v}p_{v}(\Gamma),

where the sum is over all vertices of the graph
\Gamma\in\mathsf{GK}_{g,0}
, and
p_{v}(\Gamma)
is obtained from
\Gamma
by attaching a leg labeled by
1
to vertex
v
. If the old decoration of
v
is
\alpha\in H^{i}(\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{h,k})
, then the new decoration on the vertex is given by
\pi^{*}\alpha\in H^{i}(\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{h,k+1})
, with
\pi\colon\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{h,k+1}\to\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{h,k}
forgetting the new marking. To see this, note that if
\Gamma
has
j
edges then the underlying graphs of
p_{v}(\Gamma)
, obtained by attaching a leg labeled
1
to a vertex
v
of
\Gamma
, correspond precisely to the strata of codimension
j
that map onto the codimension
j
stratum
\xi_{\Gamma}({\mathcal{M}}_{\Gamma})\subset\overline{{\mathcal{M}}}_{\Gamma}
, and the operation on decorations that we have described corresponds, via the Künneth decomposition, to the induced pullback on the cohomology of strata in the simplicial resolution.

The same formula (
53
) also defines a pullback operation

\pi^{*}\colon\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,0}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,1},

and the projection map
\mathsf{GK}_{g,n}\to\overline{\mathsf{GK}}{}_{g,n}
intertwines the two operations
\pi^{*}
.
We furthermore define another operation

\varpi^{*}\colon(H_{g},\tilde{\delta})\to(X^{\star}_{g,1},\tilde{\delta})

by taking minus the disjoint union with an
(\epsilon,1)
-edge,

\varpi^{*}\colon\hbox to19.08pt{\vbox to19.08pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 9.53984pt\lower-9.53984pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 12.92 0 C 12.92 7.14 7.14 12.92 0 12.92 C -7.14 12.92 -12.92 7.14 -12.92 0 C -12.92 -7.14 -7.14 -12.92 0 -12.92 C 7.14 -12.92 12.92 -7.14 12.92 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

Proof sketch.

A graph
\Gamma\in H_{g}
contains either no
\epsilon
-leg, or exactly two, on an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge.
We consider both cases in turn.
Suppose first that
\Gamma\in H_{g}
contains no
\epsilon
-leg.
Then its image under the first two horizontal maps in (
54
) is just the same unaltered graph
\Gamma
.
Applying
F
produces the linear combination (
50
). Applying
\pi^{*}
afterwards produces a linear combination of graphs of the form

(55)

In the first two sums one sums over all ways of attaching the
1
-labeled leg to a vertex, including the special vertex.
Here we are using
[
2
, Proposition 3.1 (ii)]
to compute the pullback of the
\psi
-class, and the additional
\delta_{0,S}
-terms there produce the last two summands.
To compare, let us now follow our graph
\Gamma
along the lower rim of (
54
).
The vertical arrow
\varpi^{*}
adds one
(\epsilon,1)
-edge to
\Gamma
. Call the resulting graph
-\Gamma^{\prime}\in X^{\star}_{g,1}
.
Applying
\Xi
then produces
\Gamma^{\prime}
plus the sum of all graphs obtained by attaching a
1
-labeled leg to
\Gamma
.
Applying
F
produces from this latter sum the two sums in (
55
).
Applying
F
to
\Gamma^{\prime}
produces the last two summands in (
55
) via (
51
).
This shows commutativity of (
54
) for
\Gamma\in H_{g}
without
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge.
The proof in the case where
\Gamma\in H_{g}
has an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge is essentially similar, although the map
\Xi
produces more terms in presence of an
(\epsilon,\epsilon)
-edge.
∎
